beats.intro: Chapter three. [[sub]]Ratios turn a pile of statements into answers. This chapter shows which ratio answers which question.
beats.process: Financial analysis is a process, not a formula. [[s1]]First, state the purpose and context. [[s2]]Collect the data. [[s3]]Process it into statements and ratios. [[s4]]Analyze and interpret the results. [[s5]]Develop and communicate conclusions. [[s6]]And follow up, because the answer may need updating. [[note]]Computing a ratio is not analysis. Analysis explains what the numbers mean for the question you started with.
beats.commonsize: Common-size statements divide every line by revenue. [[a]]Company A spends sixty percent of revenue on cost of sales, twenty five on selling and administration, three on interest, three point six on tax, and keeps eight point four as net income. [[b]]Company B spends seventy on cost of sales, but only fourteen on selling and administration, and keeps nine point eight. [[note]]The bottom lines look similar, but the cost structures are very different. Common-size figures make that visible, and let you compare companies of any size.
beats.trend: Trend analysis follows one company over time. Set year one to one hundred. [[rev]]Revenue climbs steadily, to one twenty five. [[ni]]Net income moves much more, ending at one seventy. [[why]]Fixed costs make profit swing more than sales. The trend shows the pattern. Then you ask why.
beats.categories: Ratios fall into five families. [[a]]Activity: how efficiently assets are used. [[l]]Liquidity: can the company pay short-term bills? [[s]]Solvency: can it carry its debt over the long run? [[p]]Profitability: how much it earns on sales and on capital. [[v]]And valuation: what the market pays per unit of earnings or assets. This chapter works through the first four.
beats.activity: Activity ratios measure how fast assets turn into sales and cash. [[inv]]Inventory: cost of sales of thirty six fifty, over average inventory of four hundred, gives a turnover of about nine. In days, that is forty days of inventory on hand. [[rec]]Receivables: revenue of fifty four seventy five, over average receivables of six seventy five. Days sales outstanding: forty five. [[pay]]Payables: the company takes thirty days to pay its suppliers. [[ccc]]Put them together. Cash goes into inventory, and comes back from customers after forty plus forty five days, but suppliers fund thirty of those days. The cash conversion cycle is fifty five days. Shorter is better.
beats.liquidity: Liquidity ratios ask: can the company pay what it owes within a year? Current liabilities are five hundred. [[ca]]Current assets are seven fifty: cash one hundred, short-term investments fifty, receivables two fifty, inventory three hundred, and prepaid expenses fifty. [[cur]]Current ratio: seven fifty over five hundred, one point five. [[quick]]The quick ratio leaves out inventory and prepaids: four hundred over five hundred, zero point eight. [[cash]]The cash ratio uses only cash and investments: one fifty over five hundred, zero point three. [[note]]Each step is stricter. A healthy current ratio with a weak quick ratio means the company depends on selling its inventory.
beats.solvency: Solvency ratios ask whether a company can carry its debt. [[bs]]Here, assets of one thousand are financed by four hundred of debt and six hundred of equity. [[da]]Debt to assets is zero point four. Debt to equity is zero point six seven. [[cov]]Coverage looks at earnings. EBIT of one fifty against interest of thirty is five times. [[note]]Higher debt ratios, and lower coverage, both mean more financial risk.
beats.profit: Profitability ratios compare profit with sales, and with capital. [[gm]]Of each hundred of revenue, forty remains after cost of sales. That is the gross margin. [[om]]After selling and administration, fifteen remains. The operating margin. [[nm]]After interest and tax, eight point four. The net margin. [[ret]]Against capital: with assets of one thousand, net income of eighty four is a return on assets of eight point four percent. With equity of six hundred, it is a return on equity of fourteen percent.
beats.dupont: DuPont analysis breaks return on equity into five factors. [[tax]]Tax burden, zero point seven. [[int]]Interest burden, zero point nine. [[ebit]]EBIT margin, five point two nine percent. Multiply those three, and you have the net margin, three point three three percent. [[turn]]Asset turnover, one point one one, gives a return on assets of three point seven percent. [[lev]]Financial leverage, one point six, lifts it to a return on equity of five point nine two percent. [[note]]Now you can see which lever drives ROE: taxes, borrowing costs, operating margin, efficiency, or leverage.
beats.limits: Ratios need context. [[a]]Different accounting methods distort comparisons. [[b]]A company with several business lines blends different ratios together. [[c]]Industry norms differ: a good ratio in one industry is poor in another. [[d]]And the economic cycle matters. Ratios improve in booms and weaken in recessions. [[note]]So compare against peers, against history, and against the company's own goals.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]Common-size and trend statements show structure and direction. [[w2]]Activity, liquidity, solvency and profitability ratios each answer a different question. [[w3]]The cash conversion cycle is days of inventory, plus days of sales outstanding, minus days of payables. [[w4]]DuPont analysis splits return on equity into tax, interest, margin, efficiency and leverage.
